name: Enlicitide
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in July 2026 on two 52-week placebo-controlled phase 3 trials with more than 3,200 participants combined. Whether it prevents heart attacks and strokes is still being tested in a separate outcomes trial.
summary: Enlicitide (Lipfendra) is the first PCSK9 inhibitor taken as a daily pill. It lowered LDL cholesterol by about 56 to 59% against placebo in phase 3.
keyTakeaway: Enlicitide is a ring-shaped peptide from Merck that blocks PCSK9, a protein that makes the liver clear less LDL cholesterol. Earlier drugs aimed at this target are all injections; enlicitide is a once-daily tablet, sold as Lipfendra since its FDA approval in July 2026. In the 2,904-person CORALreef Lipids trial, LDL fell 57% from baseline on the drug while it rose 3% on placebo, and side effects were about as common as with placebo. The tablet has to be taken on an empty stomach. It is not yet known whether it reduces heart attacks or strokes; that trial is still running.

blocks.text: Enlicitide is a prescription drug that lowers LDL cholesterol, the kind that builds up in artery walls. It belongs to the PCSK9 inhibitor class, which until 2026 consisted only of injected antibodies and an injected RNA drug. Enlicitide is instead a macrocyclic peptide (a chain of amino acids closed into a ring), small and stable enough to be swallowed as a tablet [2].

Merck developed it under the code MK-0616 and sells it in the United States as Lipfendra. Each film-coated tablet holds 20 mg of the drug, supplied as a salt called enlicitide decanoate [2]. The label lists no contraindications, meaning no group of patients in whom it is ruled out outright [2].

Liver cells carry LDL receptors that grab LDL particles from the blood and pull them inside. A circulating protein called PCSK9 attaches to these receptors and steers them toward breakdown, so fewer receptors remain to do the clearing. Enlicitide binds PCSK9 and stops it from latching onto the receptor, which leaves more receptors working and lowers the amount of LDL in circulation [2].

Getting a peptide through the gut is the hard part. Only about 1% of each dose reaches the bloodstream, helped by sodium caprate, an ingredient in the tablet that eases absorption across the intestinal wall [2]. Food gets in the way: taking the tablet 30 minutes after a meal cut blood levels roughly in half in the label's studies. For that reason the label directs patients to swallow it whole in the morning with water, black coffee or plain tea, then wait at least 30 minutes before eating [2]. Levels settle into a steady state after about a week of daily use [2].

Yes. Merck announced on July 16, 2026 that the FDA had approved Lipfendra as an add-on to diet and exercise for lowering LDL cholesterol in adults who have high cholesterol, the inherited heterozygous familial form among them [3]. Merck described it as the first PCSK9 inhibitor approved in pill form [3].

The approval rests on LDL lowering, a measurement, rather than on proof of fewer cardiovascular events. A third phase 3 trial, CORALreef Outcomes, had enrolled more than 14,500 people at the time of approval and is testing whether the drug reduces heart attacks, strokes and deaths. Until it reports, that benefit is unproven for enlicitide itself [3].

blocks.text: Enlicitide is prescribed to bring down LDL cholesterol in adults whose levels stay too high, including people with the inherited condition HeFH, in which a gene variant keeps LDL elevated from birth [2]. In the pivotal trials it was added on top of existing treatment, mostly statins, in people who had already had a heart attack or stroke or were judged at raised risk of a first one [1].

In CORALreef Lipids, 2,909 adults were randomized two to one to enlicitide or placebo for 52 weeks. At week 24, LDL had fallen 57.1% from baseline on enlicitide and risen 3.0% on placebo, a gap of about 56 percentage points. Non-HDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B and lipoprotein(a), other markers tied to artery disease, also dropped more on the drug [1]. In the separate HeFH trial of 303 adults, the week-24 reduction against placebo was 59% [3].

CORALreef AddOn compared enlicitide directly with other cholesterol pills in 301 statin-treated adults over 56 days. LDL fell 64.6% with enlicitide, against 27.8% with ezetimibe, 6.3% with bempedoic acid and 36.5% with the two combined [4].

blocks.text: In the larger trial, side effects showed up at about the same rate on enlicitide as on placebo, and similar shares of each group stopped treatment because of one [2]. In the HeFH trial, the two reactions that appeared more often on the drug were dizziness (9% versus 4% on placebo) and diarrhea (7% versus 2%) [3].

The label advises stopping enlicitide once a pregnancy is recognized unless the benefit is judged to outweigh the risk. The reason is the mechanism: lowering cholesterol may also lower substances the fetus builds from cholesterol, and there are not enough human pregnancy data to judge the risk directly. Animal studies at many times the human exposure did not show harm to developing offspring [2]. The full prescribing information covers interactions and other details.
